paragraphs.title: The Oppression of the Wealthy and the Coming Punishment

easy.explanation: Amos calls them "ye kine of Bashan."
easy.q: What does the prophet call the women of Samaria?

easy.explanation: They oppress the poor and crush the needy.
easy.q: Whom do these women oppress and crush?

easy.explanation: They say, "Bring, and let us drink."
easy.q: What do they say to their masters?

answers: They are prosperous but still mistreat the poor
They give all their possessions to the poor
medium.explanation: Their luxury is joined with oppression of the poor and needy.
medium.q: Why is their oppression especially serious?

answers: They will be taken away with hooks and fishhooks
medium.explanation: The Lord says that He will take them away with hooks and fishhooks.
medium.q: What punishment does the Lord announce for them?

answers: Poor women working in the fields
medium.explanation: The phrase pictures the luxurious women of Samaria as fat cattle from Bashan.
medium.q: What does the phrase "kine of Bashan" suggest in this passage?

answers: The women's luxury versus the suffering of the poor
challenge.explanation: The passage contrasts their comfortable lives with their oppression of the poor.
challenge.q: What central contrast does this passage emphasize?

answers: That their luxurious living is connected with coming judgment
That drinking was a special commandment
challenge.explanation: Their self-indulgence is followed by a humiliating punishment.
challenge.q: What does the movement from "let us drink" to captivity show?

answers: They will remain safely in the city
They will be taken out through the breaches and cast into the palace
They will be given abundant food
challenge.explanation: They are forcibly led out through the breaches and cast away.
challenge.q: What detail is easy to miss in the description of their punishment?

paragraphs.title: Corrupted Worship That Cannot Atone for Sin

easy.explanation: The passage names Bethel and Gilgal.
easy.q: To which places are the people told to go?

easy.explanation: They are told to bring their sacrifices every morning.
easy.q: What are they told to bring every morning?

easy.explanation: They are told to proclaim and publish the free offerings.
easy.q: What are they told to proclaim and publish?

medium.explanation: The commands to come and transgress show prophetic irony.
medium.q: What is the prophet's attitude toward this worship?

answers: It continues alongside transgression and disregards God's requirements
They had no places of worship
medium.explanation: Their religious actions occur while they continue in sin.
medium.q: Why can this worship not make up for their sin?

answers: Offerings or portions set apart from produce
medium.explanation: Tithes are portions of goods or produce set apart as offerings.
medium.q: What does "your tithes after three years" refer to?

answers: The worship itself is presented as part of their sin
The people are shown to have stopped sinning
The worship is presented as a military event
challenge.explanation: The prophet links their religious activity directly with transgression.
challenge.q: What effect is created by the words "transgress" and "multiply transgression"?

answers: Proclaiming and publishing the free offerings
challenge.explanation: The passage specifically says to proclaim and publish the offerings.
challenge.q: Which detail emphasizes their desire to make their religious acts known?

answers: Many offerings cannot compensate for continuing sin
Only one sacrifice is allowed each year
challenge.explanation: The problem is not merely the number of offerings but the sinful worshiper's heart and conduct.
challenge.q: What is the main message about their sacrifices?

easy.explanation: The Lord gave them "want of bread in all your places."
easy.q: What shortage came upon the cities?

easy.explanation: The Lord says, "I have withholden the rain from you."
easy.q: What did the Lord withhold from the people?
What devoured the gardens, vineyards, fig trees, and olive trees?

answers: Rain fell equally on every city
Rain fell on one city but not on another
No rain fell anywhere for a full year
medium.explanation: The Lord caused rain on one city and withheld it from another.
medium.q: How is the lack of rain described?

answers: To drink water, though they were not satisfied
medium.explanation: They went to another city for water but were not satisfied.
medium.q: Why did two or three cities wander to one city?

answers: Hunger caused by lack of food
Cleaning the teeth after a meal
medium.explanation: The phrase pictures empty mouths because there was no bread.
medium.q: What does the phrase "cleanness of teeth" mean here?

answers: The people returned unto the Lord
The people did not return unto the Lord
challenge.explanation: The Lord repeatedly says, "yet have ye not returned unto me."
challenge.q: What statement is repeated after the punishments?

answers: Hunger, drought, lack of water, crop damage, pestilence, war, and overthrow
War, prosperity, rain, building, and celebration
Exile, kingship, peace, harvest, and abundance
challenge.explanation: The passage lists these judgments one after another.
challenge.q: Which sequence best summarizes the punishments in this passage?

answers: They were warnings meant to lead the people to repentance, but the people did not repent
The people gladly accepted every punishment
The punishments were merely descriptions of weather
challenge.explanation: The repeated warnings show that the people still failed to return to God.
challenge.q: What can be inferred from the variety and repetition of the punishments?

easy.explanation: The command is, "prepare to meet thy God, O Israel."
easy.q: For what is Israel told to prepare?

easy.explanation: He forms the mountains and creates the wind.
easy.q: What does the Lord form and create?

answers: The LORD, The God of hosts
easy.explanation: The passage ends, "The LORD, The God of hosts, is his name."
easy.q: What name is given at the end of the passage?

answers: It follows the repeated failure of the people to return to God
medium.explanation: After the people refuse to return, they are told to prepare to meet God.
medium.q: How is the command to prepare related to the earlier punishments?

medium.explanation: The Lord makes the morning darkness.
medium.q: Which contrasting conditions appear in the description of the Lord's power?

answers: The Lord rules over the heights and all the earth
The Lord builds houses on mountains
The Lord travels between Israelite cities
medium.explanation: The phrase emphasizes the Lord's authority over the earth.
medium.q: What does "treadeth upon the high places of the earth" communicate?

answers: It speaks only of the beauty of nature
It presents the Lord as possessing absolute power after the people's refusal to return
challenge.explanation: The final description of God's power follows repeated warnings and judgments.
challenge.q: What makes the ending of the chapter threatening?

answers: He declareth unto man what is his thought
challenge.explanation: The Lord declares a person's thought, showing His knowledge of the inner life.
challenge.q: Which detail shows that the Lord knows what is hidden in a person?

answers: God's vast power makes meeting Him serious and fearful
It proves that the people have already repented
It explains how to grow crops
challenge.explanation: The Lord's power over creation makes the coming encounter solemn and daunting.
challenge.q: How does the description of creation support the command to prepare?
